lesson.title: The Americas
lesson.summary: Maya cities, Mexica tribute, Inca labor, and diverse North American communities.
learningGoals: Explain continuity and change in American state building.
Use evidence to distinguish Maya cities, Mexica tributary rule, and Inca administration.
lesson.bigIdea: American societies built cities and states using local crops, labor obligations, sacred authority, and regional exchange. Maya, Mexica, Inca, and North American communities developed distinct institutions.
lesson.context: The Classic Maya period largely preceded 1200, but Maya communities and cities continued afterward. Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325 and the Mexica Triple Alliance formed in 1428. Inca expansion accelerated around 1438 under Pachacuti. Their later imperial peaks and the Spanish conquests belong partly or entirely after this unit’s endpoint.

sections.title: Maya cities continued a long tradition.
sections.conceptTitle: Maya cities continued a long tradition.

blocks.text: Maya political life often centered on city-states, each joining an urban center to surrounding communities. Rulers competed, made alliances, demanded tribute, and used warfare to pursue power. No single government permanently united all Maya peoples.

Rulers connected their authority with ancestry and sacred ritual. Scribes recorded dynastic events, while calendrical and astronomical knowledge helped organize ceremonies. Writing and mathematics served political and cultural needs as well as intellectual inquiry.

Many southern lowland centers had declined before 1200, yet cities such as Mayapan remained important in the later period. Changes in major settlements should not be mistaken for the disappearance of Maya peoples, whose communities and languages continue today.

sections.takeaway: Distinguish a city’s decline from the end of an entire people or culture.

sections.title: Mexica rule linked tribute to military power.
sections.conceptTitle: Mexica rule linked tribute to military power.

blocks.text: The Mexica were central to the alliance often called the Aztec Empire. Their capital, Tenochtitlan, stood in the Lake Texcoco basin. Chinampas were constructed growing beds in shallow lake areas, separated by channels. They increased productive farmland near a dense urban population; they were not gardens drifting freely on the lake.

Conquered communities supplied goods such as food and textiles. Local rulers could remain in place if they met obligations, while imperial demands were backed by force. This arrangement allowed the alliance to draw resources from many communities without replacing every local institution.

Markets and merchants also mattered alongside tribute. Nobles and warriors enjoyed privileges, while commoners supplied much of the farming and craft labor. State rituals and sacred authority helped legitimize rulers and warfare, including ceremonies involving human sacrifice. Tribute burdens and coercion could generate resistance.

sections.takeaway: Tribute was an obligation imposed on subject communities. It was different from voluntary buying and selling, even though both existed.

sections.title: Inca administration mobilized people and resources.
sections.conceptTitle: Inca administration mobilized people and resources.

blocks.text: The Inca expanded outward from Cusco in the Andes, especially during the fifteenth century. Officials worked through local communities and leaders to organize resources. The ayllu, a community linked through kinship and reciprocal obligations, was an important foundation of social organization.

Mit’a was a rotating labor obligation owed to the state. Work could support farming, construction, or military needs. The state collected and redistributed supplies through storehouses, connecting labor duties to its capacity to govern. This was not the same as a wage contract or the later Spanish colonial mining system.

Roads, bridges, and relay messengers helped move information and supplies through difficult terrain. Khipus, also spelled quipus, used knotted cords to record information such as quantities and obligations. These tools supported a complex administration even without an alphabetic writing system.

The ruler’s association with Inti, the sun deity, and the honoring of royal ancestors reinforced authority. Local sacred places and traditions continued within the empire. Imperial integration involved negotiation and coercion, not just willing cultural unity.

sections.takeaway: Connect the institution to the outcome: labor duties and records helped the state organize projects, supplies, and subject populations.

sections.title: Farming techniques answered different environmental problems.
sections.conceptTitle: Farming techniques answered different environmental problems.

blocks.text: In the Andes, terraces converted slopes into more manageable farming surfaces, while irrigation and local crop knowledge supported production. Potatoes and maize grew in different ecological settings. Raised-field techniques also existed in the wider Andean region, but a raised field and a hillside terrace are not the same structure.

Chinampas made use of wet environments in central Mexico. Southwestern North American communities instead developed practices for collecting and conserving scarce water. Comparing these techniques shows that productive agriculture did not require an identical environment or a single borrowed invention.

sections.takeaway: Name the environmental constraint, identify the adaptation, and explain its effect on production or settlement.

sections.title: North America contained varied political communities.
sections.conceptTitle: North America contained varied political communities.

blocks.text: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was a major Mississippian center. Maize farming supported a substantial population, regional exchange, and large earthen mounds. Differences in buildings and burials provide evidence of social ranking and organized labor.

Ancestral Pueblo communities at Chaco and Mesa Verde built substantial settlements and maintained regional connections. Chaco’s greatest influence largely preceded 1200; Mesa Verde cliff dwellings flourished during the thirteenth century. Drought, resource pressures, and social changes contributed to relocation, with the importance of individual causes debated.

Their descendants include living Pueblo communities. Use archaeology and Indigenous knowledge together, and do not interpret migration as the mysterious disappearance of a people. European conquest cannot explain changes that occurred centuries before European arrival in these regions.

sections.takeaway: Monumental construction can support a claim about coordinated labor, but by itself it does not reveal an exact constitution or every ruler’s identity.

vocabulary.definition: An independent political center joining a Maya city with surrounding communities.
The people centered at Tenochtitlan who became dominant partners in the Aztec Triple Alliance.
Required payments, often in goods, from subordinate communities to a ruling power.
Constructed agricultural beds in shallow lake areas, divided by water channels.
Mexica capital founded in 1325 in the Lake Texcoco basin.
An Inca ruler associated with rapid imperial expansion beginning around 1438.
An Andean community linked through kinship and reciprocal obligations.
A rotating labor obligation used by the Inca state to obtain work from subject households.
Knotted cords used for recording information, including quantities and obligations.
Cultivation on stepped surfaces built into slopes.
A major Mississippian settlement known for large mounds and regional exchange.
Communities of the American Southwest whose descendants include living Pueblo peoples.

connections.title: Goods and labor
connections.body: Mexica tribute and Inca mit’a both supported rulers, but one emphasized required goods while the other mobilized rotating labor. Explain what each let the state do.

connections.title: Adaptation and settlement
connections.body: Chinampas used wet lake environments; terraces made slopes more manageable. Both helped communities produce food under different local conditions.

connections.title: Evidence and limits
connections.body: Mounds, roads, and storehouses show coordinated effort. They cannot alone identify every official, motive, or belief. Combine material evidence with other sources.
